chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: Buster Bailey, the fastest clarinetist from Memphis
summary: Crawford praises Buster Bailey, who played with W. C. Handy, as the greatest clarinetist, better than Benny Goodman.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: And another fellow I was very, very much engrossed in, which I figured was the fastest clarinetist in the world, that was a homey -- hometowner by the name of Buster Bailey. You see, his father disallowed him to play with any other band other than W. C. Handy's. He was the original St. Louis Blues player. He was sitting in the band. He was working with Handy because his father didn't -- didn't want him to go out of town and didn't want him to quit school, going to [Cotchard] High School in Memphis.

He -- I didn't know Buster in Memphis, to be frank with you. And along came Buster with W. C. Handy and the St. Louis Blues, and he was one of the first ones to play St. Louis Blues, and that man to me was the greatest clarinetist in the world. That included all of them. Benny Goodman was -- which Benny can really play. That rascal can play, with the help of John Hammond, of course. And --
